sections.h2: Tax office, Supervisors and Chancery Clerk
sections.html:
One office does both tax jobs in Hancock County, and the County Administrator holds the Tax Assessor and Collector role too. It operates from 854 Highway 90, Bay St. Louis, phone (228) 466-5791. A Tax Assessor page on the county site links to tax and fee details and a homestead exemption page.

  • Board of Supervisors: 854 Highway 90, Suite A, Bay St. Louis, phone (228) 467-0172.
  • Chancery Clerk and land records: 854 Highway 90, Suite B, phone (228) 467-5404.
  • Appeals of an assessment go to the Board of Supervisors, with the Chancery Clerk as the contact.

Call the office before you pay or mail a check, and confirm hours and payment methods.

Five constitutional classes sort Mississippi property, and each county follows them. The tax is true value, times the class ratio, times millage. Levies come separately from the county, each city and the school district, so a Diamondhead house and a house in unincorporated Kiln can carry different totals.

Mississippi property classes and ratios
ClassPropertyRatio
IOwner-occupied single-family home10%
IIOther real property15%
IIIPersonal property15%
IVPublic utilities30%
VMotor vehicles30%

For an official millage number, the Department of Revenue property tax data page lists combined county and city rates for 2012 through 2025. By law the assessor must revalue real property every four years at minimum, and there is no requirement to go inside your house.

Your tax belongs to the person who holds the parcel on January 1, and the payment date is February 1. Statements arrive in November and December. When that date lands on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, the following Monday is still penalty-free.

Unpaid real property can be sold at the county tax sale, after which the former owner keeps two years to redeem under Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3. A parcel that draws no buyer passes to the State, and the Secretary of State deals with it at 1-866-835-2637.

Sellers should get a current payoff, plus any balance from earlier years, before agreeing to a contract. Title companies refuse to close over unpaid delinquent tax, so the order of operations matters: find out first, then price the house.

Disagree with a value? Request a hearing in front of the Board of Supervisors through the Chancery Clerk. File by the first Monday in August, which is before the bill is due, so waiting for the December statement is too late.

Document what you can. A storm-damaged roof or a wrong square footage on the record is worth photographing. When an appraisal used inaccurate information about the size of a home, a refund of earlier years may be possible, and the Chancery Clerk can walk you through it.

Anyone moving in must apply for homestead under their own name, so the seller should not assume the exemption carries over. The Tax Assessor takes applications January 1 through April 1, and the filing normally stands until something about your status changes.

Owners 65 or older, and totally disabled owners who otherwise qualify, owe nothing on the first $75,000 of true value. The exemption is lost when the owner or spouse is behind on state income tax, or when a vehicle is tagged in a county other than the home's. If you have moved out, stop claiming homestead on the old house.

Hurricane Katrina made its final landfall here on August 29, 2005, and local buyers still ask how a house fared. The storm destroyed nearly the entire first block off the beach, and homes as far as 10 miles inland flooded. Highway 603 south of Interstate 10 was submerged and the Highway 90 bridge at Bay St. Louis was wrecked. Bay St. Louis, Waveland, Pearlington, Diamondhead and Kiln all took heavy damage.

  • A buyer's insurer and lender will ask about flood zone and elevation, and a house with past water damage can be hard to finance.
  • Water covers 14% of the county's area, so many parcels sit near the shore. Check the county or FEMA flood maps to see where yours falls.
  • A cash buyer who purchases as-is can skip repair and insurance hurdles that sink conventional contracts, but should still be told about any known damage.

Your house may have storm or flood history, may be inherited, or may have sat empty. Each case calls for its own paperwork.

  1. Locate the deed and last tax statement, and check whose name is on the roll.
  2. Request any earlier-year balance from the Tax Assessor and Collector.
  3. Ask the Chancery Clerk whether a tax sale is recorded on the parcel.
  4. Collect repair and insurance records so a buyer can price the house fairly.

With a cash sale the buyer accepts the house as it stands. Clear title and settled current-year tax on the closing statement are still required. Verify each figure with the county office before relying on it.

sections.h2: Steps to take before you list
sections.html:
Start at the combined tax office on Highway 90 and ask for the parcel's current balance and any earlier year still open. If you inherited the house, make sure the roll shows the right owner, because a bill that goes to a deceased relative is still due. Then stop at the Chancery Clerk's suite in the same building to confirm that no tax sale is recorded against the parcel and that your deed is on file.

With those answers in hand, think about condition. Buyers and their insurers will want to know the flood zone and any history of water damage, so pull repair receipts and insurance papers early. A cash buyer can overlook cosmetic problems, but the title still has to be clear and the tax record settled. Finally, ask the title company to add the payoff to the closing statement so the county is paid out of your proceeds and nothing follows you after the sale.

Hancock County sits on the Gulf of Mexico at the Louisiana line, and its county seat is Bay St. Louis. It covers 553 square miles, and 79 of them (14%) are water, so much of the county is bayou, bay and marsh. The 2020 census counted 46,053 people.

The three cities are Bay St. Louis, Diamondhead and Waveland. Kiln and Pearlington are census-designated places, and smaller communities include Lakeshore, Clermont Harbor, Necaise and Napoleon. The John C. Stennis Space Center is in the county, which is part of the Gulfport-Biloxi metropolitan area. I-10, U.S. 90 and MS 43, 53, 603 and 607 are the major routes. School districts are Bay St. Louis, Hancock County and Picayune.

faqs.q: When are Hancock County property taxes due?
faqs.a: February 1. When it falls on a weekend or holiday, the next Monday is penalty-free.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Hancock County?
faqs.a: A single combined Tax Assessor and Collector office, run by the County Administrator. Visit 854 Highway 90, Bay St. Louis, or call (228) 466-5791 to confirm hours and payment types.

faqs.q: How do I appeal a Hancock County assessment?
faqs.a: Request a hearing before the Board of Supervisors through the Chancery Clerk, filing by the first Monday in August, ahead of the due date.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Hancock County house damaged by a storm?
faqs.a: Yes, a cash buyer can take a damaged house as-is. You still need clear title, taxes paid or settled at closing, and honest disclosure of damage you know about.

faqs.q: How long can I redeem a Hancock County parcel after a tax sale?
faqs.a: Two years from the sale date, under Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3. Redemption notices and payments go through the Chancery Clerk.
